records.title: Translation Among Complementary Approaches for Understanding Complex Neurobehavioral Toxicology.
records.abstract: Neurobehavioral toxicology is challenged with dual missions where the field must determine toxic risks to the functionality of a very complex organ while also doing so a scale of tens of thousands of potentially neurotoxic chemicals. Classic mammalian models of neurobehavioral toxicology can determine, in great detail, toxic chemical risks to complex neurobehavioral functions such as emotion and cognition. However, such studies are expensive and slow, and relatively few chemicals can be tested. High throughput in vitro assessment can provide important information concerning toxicity in neurons and other relevant cell types. However, the brain is an organ of communication, so neurotoxicity affecting functions such as emotional function and cognition need more complex model systems to determine neurotoxic risks on these functions. New developments in multi-cellular 2D, 3D, or organoid in vitro systems, invertebrate organisms, and aquatic vertebrate species such as zebrafish offer a spectrum of approaches to bridge the gap between chemical effects on key neurodevelopmental processes and complex interactions in neural systems. This article proceeds from a symposium at the INA-19 theme "Bridging between in vitro and in vivo to improve interpretation of neurotoxicological data." It covers sophisticated in vitro, invertebrate, and complementary vertebrate models to explore neurotoxicological risk across the lifespan and how functional deficits relate to mammalian models. Bridging between in vitro and in vivo systems will help determine neurotoxic risks on complex neurobehavioral function, including relevance to neurotoxic consequences in humans.

records.title: Organoid-based reconstruction of tumor microenvironment complexity: from epithelial cores to immune ecosystems.
records.abstract: Tumor progression and therapeutic responses are shaped by complex and dynamic interactions between malignant cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME). In recent years, a wide range of advanced 3D in vitro and ex vivo model systems has been developed to capture different aspects of this complexity. However, these models are often discussed in isolation, and the concept of TME recapitulation remains variably defined across experimental platforms. In this review, we discuss how human cancer organoids can serve as a controlled epithelial platform for reconstructing TME complexity in a stepwise manner. We examine how non-immune components, including extracellular matrix properties, biophysical cues, and stromal interactions, contribute to tumor state and behavior when incorporated into organoid-based systems. We then focus on organoid-based modelling of the tumor immune microenvironment as a particularly informative example of functional TME complexity, highlighting how immune-tumor interactions and dynamic state changes can be interrogated in vitro. Finally, we place organoid-based approaches in the context of ex vivo and native tissue models, discussing their complementary strengths and limitations with respect to experimental control, fidelity to native architecture and functional interrogation. Together, this review provides a perspective on how human organoid-based platforms can serve as a foundation for reconstructing TME complexity, with ex vivo and native tissue models providing complementary context.

records.title: Epigenetic remodeling and targetable ADGRB1 drive metabolic adaptation to KRAS inhibition via fatty acid scavenging.
records.abstract: Although inhibitors of oncogenic KRAS show clinical efficacy, adaptation to KRAS inhibition (KRASi) is common, and its molecular basis remains unclear. We used transcriptomic, epigenetic, proteomic, and metabolic analyses across a series of KRASi-sensitive and -resistant cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and mouse models to elucidate the metabolic regulatory mechanisms underlying tumor adaptation to KRASi. We also evaluated novel combination therapeutic strategies in these model systems through genetic and pharmacological perturbations. Adaptation to KRASi involved SIRT1 inactivation-mediated epigenetic remodeling, which enables TFEB to transcriptionally activate lipid metabolic and mitochondrial gene programs and upregulate ADGRB1 expression, thereby establishing a persistent metabolic state across multiple KRAS-mutant cancer models despite KRAS suppression. Mechanistically, ADGRB1 acted as a promoter of fatty acid (FA) acquisition through PI3Kγ-PAK1-dependent noncanonical macropinocytosis, enabling scavenging of adipose-derived FA and sustaining adaptation to KRASi. Upregulation of the ADGRB1 axis may be associated with resistance to KRAS-targeted therapy and unfavorable clinical outcomes. Disrupting ADGRB1-PI3Kγ signaling dismantled metabolic homeostasis during KRASi. Therapeutically, an ADGRB1 tethered agonist-interfering peptide restored sensitivity to KRASi and suppressed tumor progression. ADGRB1-dependent FA scavenging represents a metabolic adaptation mechanism and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in KRAS-mutant cancers. records.title: Metabolic substrate availability regulates nephron lineage expansion in human kidney organoids.
records.abstract: Human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney organoids are widely used to model nephrogenesis; yet, variability in basal media composition remains an underappreciated source of developmental heterogeneity. We hypothesized that metabolic substrate availability directly regulates organoid development. Comparing commonly used media, we found that advanced RPMI supported robust growth and tubular expansion, whereas DMEM containing 5.0 mM glucose impaired nephron lineage development. Supplementation to 11.1 mM glucose significantly rescued these defects, demonstrating a causal role for substrate availability. Metabolomics analysis revealed rapid glucose depletion under low glucose conditions and reduced metabolic activity, while higher glucose media supported oxidative metabolism. Functionally, glucose availability directly influenced cellular proliferation and survival, with low glucose associated with increased TUNEL positivity and cleaved caspase-3. Together, these findings identify glucose as a critical regulator of kidney organoid development and position metabolic substrate composition as a tunable determinant of organoid fidelity and reproducibility.

records.title: Patient-derived organoids identify PI3K-AKT signaling as a therapeutic target in sacituzumab govitecan-resistant triple-negative breast cancer.
records.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapies and frequent resistance. Sacituzumab govitecan (SG), a TROP-2-directed antibody-drug conjugate, improves survival in metastatic TNBC, yet determinants of response remain poorly defined. Using a biobank of patient-derived organoids (PDOs), we show that SG sensitivity in PDOs predicts patient outcomes. Multi-omics profiling of SG-resistant PDOs identifies a transcriptionally plastic epithelial subpopulation enriched for PI3K-AKT signaling and pro-survival programs, which persists after treatment and drives resistance. In preclinical models, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K with alpelisib resensitizes resistant tumors to SG, restoring treatment efficacy and prolonging survival. Our findings identify PI3K-AKT signaling as a mechanism of SG resistance in TNBC and provide a rationale for PI3K-targeted combination therapy to improve SG efficacy.

records.title: Gut microbiota-metabolites-target organ axis: an emerging territory for visualizing the indirect actions of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
records.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been widely used for centuries, yet its pharmacological basis remains paradoxical: many bioactive ingredients, particularly polysaccharides, saponins, and certain alkaloids, exhibit extremely low oral bioavailability yet produce consistent systemic therapeutic effects. This paradox challenges the conventional notion that drug efficacy requires direct target engagement, highlighting the need for alternative, indirect mechanisms of action. This review aims to elucidate the gut microbiota-metabolite-target organ axis as a mechanistic basis for the indirect actions of TCM, and to synthesize recent progress in causal validation approaches that move this field from correlative observations toward causal demonstration. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases up to 2026, using keyword combinations related to gut microbiota, microbial metabolites, Traditional Chinese Medicine, indirect pharmacology, etc. Additional studies were identified by screening reference lists of eligible articles and relevant reviews. A total of 135 articles were included based on their relevance to the mechanistic focus of this review. A substantial fraction of orally administered TCM components, particularly those with low bioavailability, interact with the gut microbiota in two reciprocal directions, serving as substrates for microbial enzymatic transformation while also modulating microbial ecology. The remodeled microbiota generates intermediate metabolites, primarily short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives, which act as chemical messengers to distal organs. These metabolites engage host receptors (GPR41/43, FXR, TGR5, and AhR) in the liver, kidneys, and cardiovascular system, translating microbial signals into therapeutic outcomes. A growing body of studies has developed a stepwise validation paradigm, ranging from correlative observations and microbiota depletion/reconstitution to metabolite reconstitution and target gene manipulation, to move this axis from association toward causally verified mechanisms. Challenges including inter-individual microbiota variation, methodological standardization, and clinical translation are discussed, alongside emerging tools such as synthetic microbial communities, organoid-microbe co-culture systems, and the microbiota-epigenetics axis. This review synthesizes current evidence into a stepwise validation framework for the gut microbiota-metabolite-target organ axis as a mechanistically plausible pathway for the indirect actions of TCM. The framework provides a methodological heuristic for designing mechanistic studies, rather than establishing quantitative dominance for any single pathway across diverse TCM formulations.

records.title: SparseKG-Flow: A Virtual Cell Generative Architecture Unifying Structural Causal Models and Knowledge Graph Priors for Single-Cell Drug Perturbation Prediction.
records.abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to new drugs is essential for mechanism-aware virtual cell modeling, yet existing models often fail on unseen drugs or cell types by relying on memorized correlations rather than transferable mechanisms. SparseKG-Flow addresses this out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge as a generative architecture integrating three inductive biases: a sparse drug-effect encoder with Gumbel-Softmax gating, a heterogeneous graph adapter for drug-target-pathway knowledge, and a mechanism-guided residual flow decoder. On Tahoe-100M, it achieves Pearson r of 0.942 and 0.920 under Test-NewDrug and Test-NewCell settings, respectively, outperforming the next-best baseline by 16.6% and 14.8%. It also reduces Δ expression error by 89.0% and 91.7%, respectively, and more than doubles held-out-drug top-gene recovery (Overlap@50 = 0.210). Frozen-model evaluation on high-grade serous ovarian cancer patient data provides preliminary evidence of transfer beyond the Tahoe-100M panel. Ablations confirm all components aid OOD generalization, with the molecular knowledge adapter contributing the most. SparseKG-Flow further reorganizes pharmacological priors into interpretable, task-trained representations and highlights Abemaciclib, Capmatinib, and Gemcitabine in A549 analysis. It thus serves as both an accurate perturbation predictor and a mechanism-grounded virtual cell platform for therapeutic prioritization.

records.title: MitoLODE: a virtual mitochondrion framework with knowledge graph priors for trajectory modeling and mechanistic perturbation analysis.
records.abstract: Mitochondria play a central role in the pathogenesis of major diseases. Tracking how they evolve under disease conditions is valuable for understanding pathological mechanisms and identifying intervention windows. Existing single-cell trajectory inference methods rely on pseudotime rather than a real temporal axis, and rarely model disease and control as independent trajectories. Virtual cell methods target one-shot drug perturbation responses and do not handle the continuous temporal evolution of disease phenotypes. To address these gaps, we propose a virtual mitochondrion research paradigm. We first curate and construct MitoKG, a mitochondria-specific heterogeneous knowledge graph integrated from five authoritative databases. MitoKG contains 2549 nodes of four types and 23 019 edges of five relation types. Building on these priors, we develop MitoLODE, a conditioned dual-trajectory neural ordinary differential equation framework. MitoLODE embeds graph priors and temporal features throughout encoding, continuous-time dynamics, and decoding, modeling disease and control evolution as two coupled paths. Benchmarked against eight baselines across four datasets covering Parkinson's disease, cardiac, and pancreatic differentiation, MitoLODE leads in most settings and remains robust under low-data regimes and extrapolation to unseen time points. Two synthetic datasets with known ground truth validate its trajectory recovery under controlled conditions. Building on the trained model, we design a gradient-guided perturbation procedure that identifies potential intervention targets aligned with known Parkinson's pathology. We develop MGMI, a large language model-based reasoning module that grounds model outputs in MitoKG nodes and turns them into confidence-graded mechanistic hypotheses, which nonetheless require experimental validation.

records.title: Virtual Knockout in the Era of Generative AI: From Intracellular Networks to Spatial and Cross-Modal Functional Simulations.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation data have enabled computational models that predict intervention-associated cellular responses. This narrative review organizes explicit gene-regulatory-network simulations, latent and compositional response models, graph, optimal-transport, and dynamical approaches, foundation-model representations, and emerging spatial or cross-modal settings through a virtual-knockout lens. We distinguish representation-level ablation from causal genetic intervention and separate held-out regimes for genes, cell types or contexts, perturbation combinations, chemical structures, and doses. We compare representative methods, experimental resources, metrics, and benchmark frameworks and operationally define a prospective holographic virtual cell by its modalities, regulatory and physical constraints, intervention-conditioned outputs with calibrated uncertainty, and prospective validation requirements. The holographic virtual cell and Design-Build-Test-Learn roadmap are presented as future-facing criteria rather than as an achieved clinical capability.

records.title: Engineering of Microbial Cell Factories for Flavonoid Production: from Flavanone Platforms to Tailored Derivatives.
records.abstract: Flavonoids are valuable plant polyphenols used in foods, nutraceuticals, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals. However, their production is limited by the low abundance of many flavonoids in plants and the structural complexity that complicates chemical synthesis. Microbial cell factories provide a sustainable alternative, yet engineering requirements increase sharply from platform flavanones to oxidized and multiply tailored derivatives. This Review organizes recent advances according to product complexity, covering flavanones, oxidized flavones and flavonols, and methylated, glycosylated, and prenylated flavonoids. We examine the major constraints at each product level, including aromatic precursor and malonyl-CoA supply, enzyme activity and selectivity, redox and oxygen demands, and the regeneration of activated methyl, sugar, and prenyl donors. We further highlight the need to coordinate scaffold formation, oxidation, tailoring reactions, donor regeneration, and host metabolism rather than optimizing individual pathway steps independently. Finally, emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted strategies for enzyme engineering, demand-responsive pathway regulation, automated design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycles, and virtual-cell modeling are discussed. This product-complexity-oriented framework provides design principles for developing efficient, modular, and programmable microbial platforms for flavonoid biomanufacturing.

records.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction.
records.abstract: Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction's reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder's reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.

records.title: LeakageHunter-SCFM: Evidence-bounded dataset-lineage auditing for single-cell foundation model benchmarks.
records.abstract: To develop and evaluate LeakageHunter-SCFM, an evidence-bounded informatics framework for auditing dataset-lineage evidence and calibrating benchmark-independence claims in single-cell foundation model evaluation. LeakageHunter-SCFM extracts accessions, DOIs, URLs, and repository identifiers from manuscripts and related artifacts. The workflow canonicalizes resources, assigns dataset roles, constructs candidate overlap pairs, and applies claim ceilings before reviewer adjudication. We evaluated it in a curated development corpus, a locked retrospective external evaluation set, and a small prediction-blinded prospective proof-of-concept evaluation. The development workflow reduced 673 raw candidates to 84 filtered resource entries and 53 candidate overlap pairs. Prediction-visible reviewer forms agreed across all 140 retrospective evidence units; their historical labels yielded F1 0.842 across 132 binary-scored units. Independent prediction-blinded relabeling of all 140 units followed by third-assessor adjudication yielded precision 0.727, recall 0.667, specificity 0.910, and F1 0.696 across 136 binary-scored units. The seven-record, prediction-blinded proof of concept achieved recall 1.000 and precision 0.611 across 52 evidence units. All actionable-positive units came from one record. Restricting this analysis to full article bodies retained 50 units from five records and F1 0.759. Evidence-bounded lineage auditing supports biomedical foundation-model benchmark review by separating identifier overlap, actionable review priority, and confirmed exposure. LeakageHunter-SCFM provides a reproducible triage layer for lineage evidence and reserves claims about corpus membership and performance effects for direct supporting evidence.

records.title: Reconstructing enzyme engineering: an AI-driven paradigm shift in discovery, optimization, and creation.
records.abstract: Enzyme engineering is undergoing a fundamental transformation driven by advances in artificial intelligence, shifting from labor-intensive experimental campaigns toward data-driven, computationally guided workflows. Traditional approaches-directed evolution and rational design-have achieved landmark successes but remain constrained by the vastness of protein sequence space, the ruggedness of fitness landscapes, and the limited throughput of experimental screening cycles. This review systematically deconstructs the AI-driven methodological revolution across three core tasks of enzyme engineering: discovery, optimization, and creation. For enzyme discovery, we trace the evolution from homology-based sequence alignment (e.g., BLAST) to function-aware semantic retrieval powered by protein language models (PLMs), highlighting how contextual embeddings and multimodal representations (sequence-structure-text) enable the mining of remote homologs and functionally convergent enzymes invisible to traditional tools. For enzyme optimization, we examine how zero-shot evolutionary predictions, few-shot active learning, and machine learning-guided directed evolution are replacing blind mutagenesis with predictive, fitness landscape-navigating strategies that dramatically reduce experimental burden. For de novo enzyme creation, we survey the transition from physics-based computational design to generative AI paradigms-including autoregressive models, inverse folding networks, diffusion models, and multi-track joint generation frameworks-that enable the design of functional enzymes with no natural templates. Throughout, we critically assess persistent bottlenecks, including the paucity of standardized, high-quality training data, the fidelity gap between computational scoring functions and true catalytic fitness, and the challenge of capturing protein conformational dynamics. Finally, we project future directions toward semantic-driven autonomous enzyme engineering, where natural language interfaces, AI agents, and fully automated experimental platforms converge to enable closed-loop, self-optimizing enzyme design with minimal human intervention.

records.title: Structural Determinants of Thermostability in Sweet Proteins and Rational Engineering of Heat-Stable Monellin Variants.
records.abstract: Sweet proteins are promising natural low-calorie sweeteners, but limited thermostability restricts their food-processing applications. Fifteen computational predictors were evaluated against experimental mutation data across five sweet proteins: brazzein, curculin, monellin, mabinlin, and thaumatin. Structure-based methods outperformed sequence-based approaches, with ensemble-averaged ΔΔG providing the strongest discrimination. Guided by these predictions, 17 single-chain monellin variants were characterized by differential scanning fluorimetry, revealing predominantly neutral or stabilizing effects. Methionine substitutions showed greater stabilization potential than isoleucine or leucine at structurally constrained positions, potentially reflecting the flexibility of its unbranched thioether side chain. Double-mutant analysis revealed positive epistasis between positions 4 and 23 (ε = +4.11 °C), increasing the melting temperature to approximately 74 °C. Analysis of 13262 substitutions further identified polar and charged residues as major sources of predicted destabilization, while hydrophobic substitutions, particularly methionine, favored stabilization. Residue burial modulated stabilization magnitude and reliability, informing thermostability engineering of sweet proteins.

records.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design.
records.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

records.title: Scaffold-guided generative AI for Type I photosensitizer design in hypoxic photodynamic therapy.
records.abstract: Type I photosensitizers (PSs) are attractive for photodynamic therapy (PDT) of hypoxic tumors, but their development is limited by empirical modification and library screening. Here, we develop a scaffold-guided generative AI framework that couples Type I-specific prediction with controllable molecular generation for prospective PS design. AI-assisted literature mining and molecular structure recognition were first used to construct a curated data set of 1338 PSs. Subsequently, we developed BiCAM-PS, a cross-attention model integrating molecular graphs, fingerprints, and physicochemical descriptors, which achieved an accuracy of 93.3% and an ROC-AUC of 0.9633 for Type I classification under the random split. We further established PSGenerator, a scaffold decorator that generates structurally diverse molecules around predefined attachment sites, enabling prediction-guided exploration of Type I PS chemical space. Using a redesigned tetracyclic scaffold as a test case, the framework prioritized six synthetically accessible candidates, all of which experimentally exhibited Type I characteristics. Among them, A1 showed efficient radical ROS generation, strong photostability, mitochondrial localization, and potent photodynamic activity under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions, markedly suppressing 4T1 tumor growth in vivo without obvious systemic toxicity. Together, this work establishes a data-driven framework that advances Type I PS discovery from empirical molecular modification and library screening toward prospective generative design.

records.title: Epitope-conditioned generation of T-cell receptor β-chain CDR3 candidates using a pre-trained transformer model.
records.abstract: Prioritizing T-cell receptor (TCR) candidates for defined peptide-HLA targets is an important step in TCR-based immunotherapy development, but it still relies heavily on laborious and expensive experimental screening. Recent advancements in generative artificial intelligence have demonstrated promising power in protein design and engineering. In this regard, we propose a pre-trained transformer model, termed Epitope-Receptor-Transformer (ERTransformer), for the epitope-conditioned generation of candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences. ERTransformer is built on EpitopeBERT and ReceptorBERT, which are trained using 1.9 million epitope sequences and 33.1 million TCR sequences, respectively. To demonstrate the model capability, we generate 1,000 candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for each of the five epitopes with known natural TCRs. The generated candidates show low sequence similarity to natural TCR β-chains while retaining plausible CDR3 length, amino-acid composition, and conservative substitution patterns. We further conduct wet-lab experiments using flow cytometry in defined TCR/pMHC contexts and find that the level of T cell activation induced by selected artificial TCRs is either comparable to or even surpasses that of natural ones. Our work suggests that ERTransformer can expand and prioritize candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for downstream experimental screening in defined peptide-HLA and TCR-chain contexts.

records.title: Selective suppression and biasing of chemokine receptors CCR9 and ACKR4 through targeting CCL25 with de novo miniproteins.
records.abstract: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

records.title: Integrated tissue and longitudinal ctDNA profiling reveal distinct genomic evolutionary trajectories associated with response to first-line immunotherapy and chemioimmunotherapy in advanced NSCLC patients.
records.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have become a central component of first-line treatment in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite the implementation of predictive biomarkers such as PD-L1 expression on tumor cells, treatment response remains highly heterogeneous, and the mechanisms underlying durable clinical benefit and the evolution of therapy resistance are still poorly understood. We performed integrated longitudinal genomic profiling of 520 tumor tissue and liquid biopsy samples collected from 127 patients with advanced NSCLC treated with first-line pembrolizumab-based therapy. Low-pass whole-genome sequencing (lp-WGS) and targeted sequencing were used to characterize copy number alteration (CNA) dynamics, mutational processes, and clonal evolution associated with treatment response. Longitudinal circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analyses were integrated with baseline tumor tissue profiling to compare genomic trajectories between short- and long-responders. Both short- and long-responders initially demonstrated transient molecular response characterized by broad CNA normalization and reduction of detectable variants during the first months of treatment. However, longitudinal analyses revealed major differences in evolutionary dynamics between response groups. Short responders showed early shifts in subclonal architecture and expansion of resistant clonal populations, whereas long responders maintained relative evolutionary stability, with delayed diversification during therapy. Recurrent focal CNAs associated with therapy resistance included persistent amplification of the 3q22-q28 region harboring multiple oncogenic drivers, as well as alterations involving FGFR1, MYC, CCNE1, CDKN2A/B, and ICOSLG loci. Mutational analyses revealed enrichment of KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 alterations and DNA repair deficiency-associated mutational signatures in short responders, whereas long responders showed enrichment of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis and ZFHX3 alterations. Longitudinal TP53 variant allele frequency (VAF) dynamics further demonstrated persistent clonal turnover in short responders compared with a marked reduction of TP53-mutant burden in long responders. Our findings indicate that immunotherapy response in advanced NSCLC is shaped not only by baseline molecular characteristics but also by distinct evolutionary trajectories under treatment pressure. Longitudinal ctDNA profiling enables dynamic monitoring of genomic changes associated with resistant disease and may support improved stratification of patients receiving immunotherapy.

records.title: From digital pathology to integrated precision oncology: AI-driven biomarker assessment and multimodal data integration in non-small cell lung cancer.
records.abstract: Digital pathology (DP) is evolving from an image-based diagnostic modality into a quantitative platform for computational precision oncology. This transition is particularly relevant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where limited tissue specimens must support histological classification, immunohistochemistry, broad molecular profiling and an expanding range of therapy-linked biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist conventional tasks such as tissue segmentation, cell detection, quality control and biomarker quantification, but it can also derive image-based signatures associated with molecular alterations, spatial immune organization and treatment response. This review focuses primarily on NSCLC and examines the continuum from foundational image-analysis tasks and AI-assisted PD-L1 scoring to histology-based molecular prediction, computational companion diagnostics, pathology foundation models and multimodal AI. We discuss recent lung-specific evidence, including computational triage of actionable alterations, the emerging TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring paradigm and selected protein biomarkers associated with antibody-drug conjugates. We also consider the integration of pathology with genomics, transcriptomics, liquid biopsy, radiology and longitudinal clinical data. Particular attention is given to the barriers separating algorithmic performance from clinical utility: uneven adoption of whole-slide imaging, pre-analytical and scanner variability, missing or asynchronous multimodal data, propagation of upstream measurement errors, laboratory information-system interoperability, prospective validation, regulation, reimbursement and equitable access. Emerging paradigms such as digital twins and agentic AI are discussed as research directions rather than established clinical tools. We argue that the principal value of AI in NSCLC will not be autonomous diagnosis, but the reliable conversion of fragmented data streams into transparent, auditable and clinically actionable patient representations.

records.title: Interchangeability of PSMA PET Tracers and Theranostic Target Efficacy in Prostate Cancer.
records.abstract: Three prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography (PET) tracers hold FDA approval, and the theranostic agent, 177Lu-PSMA-617, given with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) is now indicated for PSMA-positive metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, in addition to its use in metastatic castration-resistant disease. Our aim is to summarize the PSMA PET tracers in clinical use and their cross validity for 177Lu-PSMA-617 target efficacy. Ga-68 PSMA-11, F-18 piflufolastat, and F-18 flotufolastat differ marginally in half-life, production, and urinary excretion, but none have shown diagnostic superiority. Pivotal trials, including VISION, PSMAfore, and PSMAddition determined eligibility with centrally read Ga-68 PSMA-11. American Society of Clinical Oncology guidance nevertheless accepts any of the three PSMA PET tracers for candidacy, and the 177Lu-PSMA-617 product label concurs. The rationale is physiologic and consensus-based: VISION defined positivity relative to liver uptake, and joint European American nuclear medicine guidance applies this rule to all tracers. Additionally, tumor/liver and tumor/salivary gland ratios are scanner-independent surrogates, supporting this cross validity. Quantitative predictors of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response and overall survival were derived using Ga-68 PSMA-11, but emerging fluorine-18 data are supportive, though there's a lack of standardization. The approved tracers appear cross-valid for liver-referenced eligibility and quantitative metrics predicting treatment response, but the strongest evidence remains tied to Ga-68 PSMA-11. Tracer interchangeability rests on consensus, rather than companion-diagnostic trials. Future randomized intra-patient comparison could potentially establish whether tracer choice alters eligibility or predicts benefit, and whether thresholds are tracer specific.

records.title: Exploratory Analysis of LDHA and PSMB4 in Extracellular Vesicles and Their Immunohistochemical Expression in Breast Tumors.
records.abstract: Introduction: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly heterogeneous tumor associated with poor prognosis and variable responses to treatment. Despite the limitations of currently available approaches for disease assessment, liquid biopsy and tumor biomarkers have emerged as promising tools for investigating molecular alterations associated with TNBC. In this context, the identification of candidate proteins and their assessment in tumor samples may provide insights into tumor biology and support the development of novel biomarkers for future clinical applications. Aim: The aim of this study was to explore candidate proteins identified by extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomic analysis and subsequently assess their expression in TNBC tumors by immunohistochemistry. Methods: Proteomic analysis of EVs derived from the blood plasma of patients with TNBC in remission and with tumor recurrence was performed as an exploratory approach to identify candidate proteins associated with recurrence. Subsequently, tumor samples from an independent cohort were evaluated by immunohistochemistry to assess the expression of the selected proteins and explore their associations with survival, histological grade, and clinical staging. The data were analyzed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Student's t-test, ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test, ROC curve analysis, and Pearson and Spearman correlations, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Results: Exploratory EV proteomic analysis identified PSMB4 and LDHA as candidate proteins detected in the recurrence group. In the independent tumor cohort, higher PSMB4 histoscore was associated with advanced clinical staging among patients in remission. LDHA expression showed discriminatory potential between TNBC and benign breast tumors, while higher LDHA expression was associated with shorter survival among patients with recurrent disease. These findings support the expression of the candidate proteins in breast tumors but do not establish their value as circulating biomarkers of recurrence. Conclusions: PSMB4 and LDHA were identified as candidate proteins through exploratory EV proteomic analysis and were subsequently assessed for expression in breast tumors by immunohistochemistry. The findings provide evidence of their expression in the tumor compartment and support further investigation of their biological and clinical relevance. However, the present study does not establish PSMB4 or LDHA as validated biomarkers of recurrence, prognosis, or diagnosis. Further studies using larger, independently defined cohorts and direct assessment of these proteins in circulating EVs are required to determine their potential clinical applicability.

records.title: Circulating MicroRNAs as Liquid Biopsy Biomarkers in Breast Cancer: Applications in Diagnosis, Prognosis, and Treatment-Related Monitoring.
records.abstract: Breast cancer remains a major global health burden, indicating the need for less invasive methods and more accurate biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are promising liquid biopsy biomarkers that can be detected in peripheral blood and may reflect tumor-associated molecular changes. This integrative literature review assessed recent evidence on circulating miRNAs in breast cancer, with emphasis on blood, plasma, and serum samples and their applications in diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment-related monitoring. The search was conducted for original studies published between 2024 and 2026. After screening and eligibility assessment, 44 studies were included. Serum was the most commonly analyzed sample, followed by plasma; RT-qPCR was the dominant detection method. Diagnostic applications were the most frequently reported, with miR-21 and miR-155 among the most consistently investigated biomarkers. Multi-miRNA panels and computational signatures generally showed higher diagnostic performance than individual miRNAs. Circulating miRNAs were also associated with disease stage, metastasis, recurrence, survival, and response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, trastuzumab, and CDK4/6 inhibitors. Nonetheless, despite these promising findings, methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, inconsistent normalization strategies, and limited external validation remain barriers to clinical applications. Standardization and prospective multicenter validation are needed to establish clinical utility.

records.title: Advances in Microfluidic-Enabled Multiplexed Profiling of Exosomal MiRNAs.
records.abstract: Exosomal miRNAs are emerging as attractive liquid-biopsy biomarkers because of their stability, specificity, and association with cancer progression. Microfluidic technologies can improve multiplex exosomal miRNAs analysis by reducing sample consumption, organizing parallel reactions, integrating extracellular-vesicle enrichment and lysis, and enabling on-chip signal decoding. This review critically compares three implementation routes-spatial encoding, bead-based encoding, and in situ detection-with emphasis on the experimentally demonstrated multiplexing level rather than theoretical coding capacity. Representative studies are compared by analyte scope, microfluidic function, target number, limit of detection, sample type, and clinical validation. Studies using total circulating miRNAs, cell or tissue lysates, non-miRNA exosomal cargoes, or in vivo imaging are explicitly identified as technology-transfer examples rather than direct demonstrations of microfluidic multiplex exosomal miRNA profiling. The remaining challenges include harmonized reporting, scalable on-chip sample preparation, robust decoding, and validation in independent clinical cohorts.
